name: James Goddard
bio: 'Kit' of George Ives's household. Cook (2014) records that he had been a servant at the Ives family seat in Hampshire and moved with George to London; on marrying he brought his wife Sylvie into the household, and their daughters were known as 'the 2 Kit girls'. He and Sylvie remained with Ives until their deaths. Ives called the household 'my little circle in the world'.
bio_sources: Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), pp. 146, 148
bio_note: Household role, Hampshire service, marriage to Sylvie and the daughters from Cook 2014, printed p. 96 (PDF 107, folio confirmed). The earlier Cook 2003 p. 146 describes him instead as 'the son of one of his father's employees' - the two accounts differ in emphasis; 2014 is the fuller treatment. That the Goddards stayed until their deaths and the daughters until the early 1940s is from Cook 2014 printed p. 100, known so far only from the PDF text layer - verify at the rendered page before quoting. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED. Cook's fullest treatment of Kit runs across printed pp. 96, 98, 100, 102, 109 and 122 (PDF 107, 109, 111, 113, 120, 133) and gives no dates: even the sentence that would most invite one - 'James and Sylvie Goddard remained with Ives until their deaths' - names no year. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. Unresolved without census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.
